summary: The BGP Monitoring Protocol in RFC 7854 defines statistics messages for observing events on a monitored router. This Standards Track document adds new statistics types for monitoring Adj-RIB-In and Adj-RIB-Out.

eli5.summary: A router keeps in and out trays of route notes. This adds new counters so watchers can see what is going into and out of the trays.

questions: what are bmp stat types 18 to 43
subtitle: New BMP counters that let a router report how many routes sit in, or were filtered from, its BGP route tables.

tldr.problem: The existing BMP statistics types give only coarse views of a monitored router, which limits route monitoring, analysis and troubleshooting.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Stat Types 18 to 23 and 26 to 43 as 64-bit Gauges for Adj-RIB-In and Adj-RIB-Out. Some are global and some are reported per address family (AFI/SAFI), and the message format is unchanged.
tldr.outcome: Operators can see current route counts before and after policy, and routes rejected, stale, suppressed, near thresholds or RPKI-validated. The RFC asks for rate limiting to protect the router.

today: RFC 9972 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why More BMP Statistics
sections.content:
The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP, RFC 7854) lets a monitored router report to a monitoring station. Section 4.8 of that RFC defines statistics types for major events, which are either counters or Gauges. RFC 8671 adds some for Adj-RIB-Out.

This document says new types are needed for more refined route monitoring and analysis, to improve operational maintenance and troubleshooting. It defines only new Gauges. The BMP Statistics Report message keeps the format from RFC 7854.
sections.eli5: Watchers of a router could only see a few simple numbers. This gives them more useful numbers to look at.

sections.title: RIBs and Policy Stages
sections.content:
A RIB is a routing information base. The RFC reuses these terms, mostly from RFC 4271.

  • Adj-RIB-In: unprocessed routing information advertised to the local BGP speaker by its peers. It has a pre-policy form (before inbound policy) and a post-policy form (after inbound policy but before route selection).
  • Adj-RIB-Out: routes for advertisement to specific peers in UPDATE messages, with pre-policy and post-policy forms around outbound policy. The post-policy form MUST convey what is actually sent to the peer.
  • Loc-RIB: routes selected by the Decision Process. As monitored through BMP it may also contain routes from other protocols such as an IGP, or local static routes.

The terms "producer" and "collector" mean the monitored router and the monitoring station.
sections.eli5: Think of an in tray for routes just arrived, an out tray for routes to send, and a best-of pile. Policy is the filter between trays.

sections.title: Statistics Format
sections.content:
Each statistic is a TLV of Stat Type, Stat Len and Stat Data; the data is called the value. Statistics come in two granularities, which may be reported at the same time.

  • Global: the value is one 64-bit unsigned Gauge and Stat Len MUST be 8. Each global statistic MUST appear only once in a report.
  • Per-AFI/SAFI: the value is 11 bytes: a 2-byte AFI, a 1-byte SAFI and a 64-bit Gauge, with Stat Len set to 11 (RFC 4760). The same (AFI, SAFI) pair MUST NOT appear twice for one statistic in a report, and entries with no data MUST NOT be included.

For statistics that apply to the Loc-RIB, the Peer Type in the Per-Peer Header MUST be 3 (Loc-RIB Instance Peer, RFC 9069). A BMP implementation MUST ignore Stat Types it does not recognize.
sections.eli5: Each number comes in a small labeled box. Some boxes hold one total, and some hold a total for each kind of route.

sections.title: The New Statistics Types
sections.content:
Types 18 to 23 and 26 to 37 cover Adj-RIB-In, and Types 38 to 43 cover Adj-RIB-Out. All are 64-bit Gauges. Groups of them are:

  • Route counts: Types 18 and 19 count the pre-policy Adj-RIB-In (global and per-AFI/SAFI), and Types 20 and 21 the post-policy one. Type 18 is like Type 7 and Type 19 is like Type 9 of RFC 7854, but explicitly pre-policy.
  • Policy results: Type 22 is routes rejected by inbound policy, and Type 23 is routes accepted. Unlike the monotonically increasing 32-bit counter of Type 0, Type 22 is the current number rejected.
  • Route state: Type 26 is routes suppressed by route flap damping (RFC 2439), Type 27 stale by Graceful Restart (RFC 4724), and Type 28 stale by Long-Lived Graceful Restart (RFC 9494).
  • Headroom: Types 29 and 30 are routes left before the received-route threshold of RFC 4271 is exceeded. Types 31 and 32 are routes left before a license-customized threshold, which MUST NOT be reported if no license or no hard limit exists.
  • AS_PATH length: Types 33 and 34 count Adj-RIB-In routes rejected for exceeding the locally supported maximum, and Types 39 and 40 count Adj-RIB-Out routes filtered for the same reason.
  • RPKI origin validation (RFC 6811): Types 35 to 37 give invalid, valid and NotFound counts for Adj-RIB-In, and Types 41 to 43 the same for Adj-RIB-Out.
  • Outbound rejects: Type 38 counts active routes that outbound policy rejected and that would otherwise have been advertised.

IANA has assigned these values in the "BMP Statistics Types" registry.
sections.eli5: Each new counter answers a question such as how many routes are in the tray, how many were thrown out, or how many are old.

sections.title: Where Each Statistic Applies
sections.content:
A table in the RFC marks each Type against five views: pre-policy Adj-RIB-In, post-policy Adj-RIB-In, Loc-RIB, pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out and post-policy Adj-RIB-Out.

Most types apply to one view only. Types 26, 27, 28, 31 and 32 apply to both post-policy Adj-RIB-In and the Loc-RIB. When reported for the Loc-RIB, Peer Type MUST be 3. Types 18, 19, 22, 33 and 34 are pre-policy Adj-RIB-In. Types 38, 39 and 40 are pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out and Types 41, 42 and 43 are post-policy Adj-RIB-Out.
sections.eli5: A chart says which counter belongs to which tray, so you do not read a number from the wrong one.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
For backward compatibility, producers able to send both Types 7 and 18, and both 9 and 19, are RECOMMENDED to send both of each pair. The choice is otherwise an implementation decision.

Statistics that depend on Graceful Restart, Long-Lived Graceful Restart or RPKI SHOULD only be generated when those features are enabled. The RFC lists Types 26 to 37 and 39 to 43 here.

Statistics may have logical links, such as per-AFI/SAFI counts summing to a global total, but implementations MAY check yet MUST NOT assume strict dependencies, because of race conditions and partial failures. A mismatch SHOULD be logged as a warning and MUST NOT disrupt protocol operation.

Reporting Types 27 and 28 during a restart costs control plane resources such as CPU, so producers SHOULD prioritize restart convergence. They MAY sample less often, buffer updates or suspend reporting. Gauges may reset after manual clearance or overflow, and producers and collectors MUST track and log such discontinuities.
sections.eli5: Counting costs effort. A busy router should do its main job first and count later, and the numbers may not always add up exactly.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
When and how new Gauges are sent is implementation dependent. Operators SHOULD choose report generation and delivery strategies, with configurable timing intervals and thresholds, and the control SHOULD match that of existing types.

Operators SHOULD rate-limit statistics updates to limit the impact on control plane processes, and enable only the statistics they need to save memory and CPU. Implementations SHOULD support per-router selection of which statistics subsets to collect and report.

Some producers may discard routes that fail policy. Then the accepted count (Type 23) and the post-policy Adj-RIB-In count (Type 21) will be identical, and operators SHOULD keep that in mind.
sections.eli5: Turn on only the counters you need, and do not ask for updates too often, or the router gets tired.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This document does not change the BMP security model. The security and authentication mechanisms in RFC 7854, RFC 8671 and RFC 9069 also apply to these Gauges, and the RFC adds no further security considerations other than one request. Monitored devices SHOULD be configured to rate-limit their reporting of the new Gauges.
sections.eli5: The same locks protect the new numbers, and the router should not send them too fast.

items.label: Pre-policy Adj-RIB-In routes
items.desc: Global count of routes now in the pre-policy Adj-RIB-In.

items.label: Post-policy Adj-RIB-In routes
items.desc: Global count of routes now in the post-policy Adj-RIB-In.

items.label: Suppressed by damping
items.desc: Per-AFI/SAFI routes suppressed by route flap damping.

items.label: Stale by GR
items.desc: Per-AFI/SAFI routes marked stale by Graceful Restart.

items.label: RPKI invalid (in)
items.desc: Per-AFI/SAFI Adj-RIB-In routes invalidated by origin validation.

items.label: Rejected by outbound policy
items.desc: Per-AFI/SAFI routes that outbound policy blocked.

items.label: RPKI NotFound (out)
items.desc: Per-AFI/SAFI Adj-RIB-Out routes with no matching ROA.
